newsitem.title: ITALY: Ethereal madonna takes to catwalk in church.
newsitem.headline: Ethereal madonna takes to catwalk in church.

text.p: An ethereal madonna dressed in a pure white chiffon gown and a trailing cloak of mottled turquoise velvet lined with scarlet floats down the catwalk, her arms outstretched and a crown of white flowers on her head.

It was to have been a crown of thorns, but Italian design house Gattinoni gave in to objections from a pro-religious group just before showing its winter 1997-98 "alta moda" (haute couture) collection in a Rome church late on Monday.
"I wanted to show beauty, purity, the things we need most," Gattinoni stylist Guillermo Mariotto told Reuters.
"This is the perfect place."

Mariotto, beaming as Rome's beautiful people filed by to kiss and congratulate him on a glowing show, said he had not minded making the change. The Lay Committee for Religious Freedom had earlier complained that his plan, the subject of much advance publicity, abused the image of the Virgin Mary.
"It drove home the message of purity not pain," he said.

Chaplain Jeffrey Evans said in a statement he had been delighted to open the doors of his All Saints Anglican Church for the collection. "To be a good Christian means enjoying one's own life and everything good it has to offer," he said.
"We must open our eyes to the beauty of divine creation."
"Beautiful" was the word that tumbled from many onlookers' lips after Mariotto's models filed down the runway in sheer chiffons, delicate beads, cobweb-fine lace and latticed silk.

The show ended on a dreamy note, to wild applause, with an elegant series of sheath hour-glass dresses featuring beaded bodices over fluid skirts in spangly white, the palest mauve, a palette of greens and burnished gold.
There were elongated, slim jackets in ivory, dove and apricot paired with floaty trousers in pleated chiffon.
Collars were dramatically upturned, or necklines enhanced with ruff-like scarves.
Full-length coats, cut wide and square to make encompassing cloaks, came in white mohair or crushed purple velvet. Others were embroidered, nipped in at the waist and split at the back.
The delicatest of fabrics, mostly in muted tones or with dramatic colours mottled or subtly blended, were mixed with applique or hand painted designs.

Multilayered handkerchief skirts, reminiscent of a flamenco dancer or a millefeuille pastry, came in blurred hues. Soft gold mingled with grey deepening to black at the edges of the swirling, but not exaggeratedly voluminous folds.
Trousers, when not wide and flowing, were pencil slim. Thigh-high boots sometimes took their place altogether.
Among innovations, Mariotto singled out the "dropped Empire line" dress -- flowing from a seam below the bust a few centimetres lower than usual. "It's a very new line," he said.

One pair of trousers flared out only at the ankle, matching the fish-tail form of one of the most dramatic dresses, a smooth black velvet creation with a white inlaid lace bodice. The neck was fastened in a neat bow with two lengths of fabric left to trail down the model's bare back.

With the runway stretching the length of the aisle, Mariotto also played on the wedding theme, pairing "grooms" in tight trousers and jackets of gold, silver and white with brides in delicate gowns finished with appliqued leaves and flowers.
Rome's fashion shows end on Wednesday with a star-studded gala on the Spanish Steps.
